title: Master Domaine Studies
description: Explore the history, philosophy, and winemaking craft of top estates including DRC, Leroy, and Rousseau
lessons.0.title: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (DRC)
lessons.0.slides.0.title: DRC: A Wine World Legend
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 1 - 20 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: Discover the birthplace of the world's most expensive wine
lessons.0.slides.1.title: DRC's Historical Heritage
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti was formally established in 1869, but its history reaches back to the 13th century. The Romanée-Conti plot was acquired in 1760 by the Prince de Conti, who outbid Louis XV's mistress Madame de Pompadour. It has carried his name ever since. Today it is co-owned by the de Villaine and Leroy-Roch families.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: DRC Historical Milestones
lessons.0.slides.3.title: 🏆 DRC's Eight Grand Crus
lessons.0.slides.3.points.2: Richebourg (3.51 ha) — DRC's most powerful, dense and complex
lessons.0.slides.3.points.3: Romanée-Saint-Vivant (5.29 ha) — most elegant and refined, silken texture
lessons.0.slides.3.points.4: Grands-Échézeaux (3.53 ha) — grand structure, requires long ageing
lessons.0.slides.3.points.5: Échézeaux (4.67 ha) — the most 'accessible' DRC, elegant with fruit
lessons.0.slides.3.points.6: Montrachet (0.67 ha) — DRC's only white, ~3,000 bottles/year, extremely rare
lessons.0.slides.3.points.7: Corton (0.48 ha) — added in 2009, from Corton Bressandes
lessons.0.slides.4.title: 📊 DRC's 8 Grand Crus: Area vs. Price
lessons.0.slides.4.content: Area ranges from 1.8 ha (RC) to 6.06 ha (La Tâche), but prices run inversely. RC is the smallest yet the most expensive — proving that rarity determines value.
lessons.0.slides.5.title: DRC's Winemaking Philosophy
lessons.0.slides.5.content: DRC moved to full biodynamic farming from 1985, making it one of Burgundy's earliest top-estate adopters. They believe only healthy soil can produce great wine. In the cellar: 100% whole-bunch fermentation, 100% new oak (from the estate's own Allier forest), no filtration or fining, and a later-than-usual bottling date.
lessons.0.slides.6.title: 🍇 DRC's Winemaking Hallmarks
lessons.0.slides.6.points.0: Ultra-low yields: just 20–25 hl/ha, well below legal limits
lessons.0.slides.6.points.2: 100% new oak: sourced from the estate's own Allier forest
lessons.0.slides.6.points.3: Long ageing: minimum 18 months in barrel
lessons.0.slides.6.points.4: No filtration or fining: preserving every terroir signal
lessons.0.slides.6.points.5: Delayed bottling: 6–12 months later than most estates
lessons.0.slides.7.title: Romanée-Conti vs. La Tâche
lessons.0.slides.8.title: Why Is DRC So Expensive?
lessons.0.slides.8.content: DRC's extraordinary prices stem from multiple factors: (1) extreme rarity — Romanée-Conti is only 1.8 ha; (2) unmatched quality consistency; (3) centuries of prestige; (4) the high cost of biodynamic viticulture; (5) demand vastly outstripping supply. A single bottle of Romanée-Conti can cost as much as a car — and prices keep rising.
lessons.0.slides.9.title: History of Romanée-Conti Prices
lessons.0.slides.10.title: 📈 Romanée-Conti: 40-Year Price Trajectory
lessons.0.slides.10.content: Prices have risen 50-fold over 40 years — an annualised return of ~10%. The rise of Asian markets (2000–2015) was the single greatest accelerant.
lessons.0.slides.11.title: DRC Monopoles vs. Shared Grand Crus
lessons.0.slides.12.title: 🎯 Three-Domaine Radar: DRC, Leroy, Rousseau
lessons.0.slides.12.content: A six-dimension comparison of DRC, Leroy, and Rousseau. DRC ranks highest in price but also in overall balance; Leroy is unmatched in concentration; Rousseau leads in quality-to-price ratio.
lessons.0.slides.13.title: 🧠 DRC In-Depth Quiz
lessons.1.title: Domaine Leroy
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Domaine Leroy: Biodynamics Taken to the Extreme
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 18 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: Explore Lalou Bize-Leroy's winemaking philosophy and radical low-yield strategy
lessons.1.slides.1.title: The Iron Lady: Lalou Bize-Leroy
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Lalou Bize-Leroy is one of Burgundy's most formidable and controversial figures. She was co-director of DRC until 1988, when she was forced out over philosophical differences. She then founded her own Domaine Leroy, pushing biodynamics to its limits. Yields are tiny, quality is staggering, and prices rival DRC.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🌿 Leroy's Biodynamic Practice
lessons.1.slides.2.points.0: Ultra-low yields: just 15–18 hl/ha (legal limit 35 hl/ha; even DRC reaches 20–25)
lessons.1.slides.2.points.1: Old vines: average vine age 50+ years; oldest 80–100 years
lessons.1.slides.2.points.2: Hand cultivation: zero chemicals, all weeding and pest control by hand
lessons.1.slides.2.points.3: Lunar calendar: all vineyard tasks timed to moon cycles
lessons.1.slides.2.points.4: Soil activation: nine biodynamic preparations including #500 (horn manure) and #501 (horn silica)
lessons.1.slides.2.points.5: Natural winemaking: wild yeast, minimal intervention, no filtration or fining
lessons.1.slides.3.title: Lalou Bize-Leroy's Career
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 🧪 Biodynamic Preparations Explained
lessons.1.slides.4.points.0: #500 (horn manure): buried in autumn, retrieved in spring — energises soil
lessons.1.slides.4.points.1: #501 (horn silica): boosts photosynthesis, strengthens plant disease resistance
lessons.1.slides.4.points.2: #502–507: compost preparations made with herbs (yarrow, chamomile, etc.)
lessons.1.slides.4.points.3: #508 (horsetail tea): prevents fungal disease, replaces chemical fungicide
lessons.1.slides.4.points.4: Applied 4–6 times per year, at specific lunar phases
lessons.1.slides.4.points.5: Dilution: 1 gram of preparation in 40 litres of water per hectare
lessons.1.slides.5.title: Domaine Leroy's Grand Crus
lessons.1.slides.5.content: Domaine Leroy holds plots in multiple top Grand Crus: Musigny, Chambertin, Clos de Vougeot, Richebourg, Romanée-Saint-Vivant, and others. Every plot is managed with extreme precision, producing wines of remarkable concentration, depth, and ageing potential.
lessons.1.slides.6.title: 🍷 Leroy's Principal Grand Crus
lessons.1.slides.6.points.0: Musigny (0.27 ha) — the most elegant and refined
lessons.1.slides.6.points.1: Chambertin (0.5 ha) — the emperor of wines
lessons.1.slides.6.points.2: Clos de Vougeot (1.91 ha) — finest upper-slope position
lessons.1.slides.6.points.5: Latricières-Chambertin (0.58 ha) — the elegant side of Chambertin
lessons.1.slides.6.points.6: Clos de la Roche (0.67 ha) — intense minerality
lessons.1.slides.7.title: Domaine Leroy vs. Maison Leroy
lessons.1.slides.8.title: Leroy's Style: Concentration and Elegance United
lessons.1.slides.8.content: Leroy's wines are famous for extreme concentration — yet they are never coarse. Ultra-low yields produce astonishing density, while biodynamic viticulture keeps the soil alive, yielding wines that combine richness with grace. Young Leroy reds need firm tannins to soften — expect 15–20 years before they reveal their full complexity and depth.
lessons.1.slides.9.title: 🧠 Domaine Leroy In-Depth Quiz
lessons.2.title: Domaine Armand Rousseau
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Armand Rousseau: King of Gevrey
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 16 minutes
lessons.2.slides.1.title: The Synonym for Gevrey-Chambertin
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Domaine Armand Rousseau was founded in 1909 and is Gevrey-Chambertin's most revered estate. Its holdings include several flagship Grand Cru plots — Chambertin, Chambertin-Clos de Bèze, and others. Current proprietor Éric Rousseau continues the family tradition, crafting wines that unite power and elegance.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 👑 Rousseau's Grand Cru Portfolio
lessons.2.slides.2.points.0: Chambertin (2.15 ha) — Napoleon's favourite; the 'Emperor of Wines'
lessons.2.slides.2.points.1: Chambertin-Clos de Bèze (1.42 ha) — equal in quality to Chambertin
lessons.2.slides.2.points.2: Clos de la Roche (1.48 ha) — sourced from Morey-Saint-Denis
lessons.2.slides.2.points.3: Mazis-Chambertin (0.53 ha) — directly adjacent to Chambertin
lessons.2.slides.2.points.4: Charmes-Chambertin (1.38 ha) — the most supple and charming
lessons.2.slides.2.points.6: Gevrey-Chambertin Clos Saint-Jacques (2.2 ha) — the finest Premier Cru
lessons.2.slides.3.title: Rousseau's Winemaking Philosophy
lessons.2.slides.3.content: Rousseau navigates a careful balance of tradition and modernity: deep respect for terroir expression, but open to useful technology. Whole-bunch fermentation at around 50–70% (adjusted to vintage), 30–50% new oak, no over-extraction. The resulting wines express Gevrey's typical structural power while retaining elegance and purity.
lessons.2.slides.4.title: 🍇 Rousseau's Winemaking Profile
lessons.2.slides.4.points.2: Cold maceration: 5–7 days at low temperature to extract aromatics
lessons.2.slides.4.points.3: Gentle extraction: avoids pulling harsh tannins
lessons.2.slides.5.title: Chambertin vs. Clos de Bèze
lessons.2.slides.6.title: Clos Saint-Jacques: The Finest Premier Cru
lessons.2.slides.6.content: Many experts consider Rousseau's Clos Saint-Jacques to equal Grand Cru quality — and to surpass many second-tier Grand Crus. This Premier Cru sits on an ideal SE-facing slope with perfectly balanced soils, producing wines of elegance, complexity, and outstanding ageing potential. The price reflects the quality, usually on a par with Grand Cru.
lessons.2.slides.7.title: Clos Saint-Jacques vs. Grand Cru
lessons.2.slides.8.title: Chambertin and the Napoleon Legend
lessons.2.slides.9.title: 🧠 Domaine Armand Rousseau Quiz
lessons.3.title: Domaine Coche-Dury: King of White Wine
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Coche-Dury: The Ultimate Standard for White Wine
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 15 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: Explore Burgundy's most legendary white wine producer
lessons.3.slides.1.title: The Hardest Burgundy to Buy
lessons.3.slides.1.content: Domaine Coche-Dury was created by Jean-François Coche-Dury, now run by his son Raphaël. Based in Meursault, the domaine specialises in white wine. Coche-Dury wines are almost entirely pre-allocated to long-standing clients — finding a bottle on the open market is nearly impossible, and prices surpass many red Grand Crus.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 🌟 Coche-Dury's Top Whites
lessons.3.slides.2.points.0: Corton-Charlemagne (0.34 ha) — the sole Grand Cru
lessons.3.slides.2.points.1: Meursault Les Perrières (0.37 ha) — closest to Grand Cru quality
lessons.3.slides.2.points.3: Meursault Les Caillerets (0.15 ha) — extremely rare
lessons.3.slides.2.points.5: Meursault Village (multiple parcels) — even this is nearly unobtainable
lessons.3.slides.3.title: The Secret of Coche-Dury's Winemaking
lessons.3.slides.3.content: Coche-Dury's success lies in an obsessive attention to detail. Near-organic viticulture, strict berry selection at harvest, wild-yeast fermentation, low new oak (20–30%), 18 months of extended lees contact, and no filtration. The wines show depth even in youth; with age, the complexity becomes extraordinary.
lessons.3.slides.4.title: 🔬 Coche-Dury Winemaking Details
lessons.3.slides.4.points.1: Low new oak: only 20–30%, to avoid overwhelming the wine with wood
lessons.3.slides.4.points.2: Extended lees ageing: 18 months with bâtonnage twice weekly
lessons.3.slides.4.points.3: Late bottling: 6 months later than most estates
lessons.3.slides.4.points.5: Low yields: strict yield control to guarantee quality
lessons.3.slides.5.title: The Legend of Meursault Les Perrières
lessons.3.slides.5.content: Many experts believe Coche-Dury's Meursault Les Perrières surpasses many white Grand Crus — some even invoke Le Montrachet. This Premier Cru sits on Meursault's upper slope, limestone soil with superb drainage. Coche-Dury's treatment of this parcel demonstrates the ultimate potential of Meursault white wine.
lessons.3.slides.6.title: Coche-Dury White Wine Winemaking Timeline (18-month cycle)
lessons.3.slides.7.title: 🍷 The Art of Bâtonnage
lessons.3.slides.7.points.0: Purpose: stir settled lees (dead yeast) back into suspension to add body and complexity
lessons.3.slides.7.points.1: Frequency: Coche-Dury does it twice weekly (in winter) — more often than most estates
lessons.3.slides.7.points.2: Timing: mainly in the 4–5 months after fermentation
lessons.3.slides.7.points.3: Effect: adds richness, creamy texture, and nutty notes
lessons.3.slides.7.points.4: Risk: over-stirring masks terroir character — precision is essential
lessons.3.slides.7.points.5: Uniqueness: Coche has mastered the perfect balance of stirring
lessons.3.slides.8.title: Coche-Dury vs. Other Meursault Masters
lessons.3.slides.9.title: 🧠 Domaine Coche-Dury Quiz
lessons.4.title: Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé
lessons.4.slides.0.title: Comte de Vogüé: Guardian of Musigny
lessons.4.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 5 - 14 minutes
lessons.4.slides.1.title: Musigny's Largest Landowner
lessons.4.slides.1.content: Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé holds 7.12 of the 7.2 hectares of Musigny Grand Cru (~70%), making it synonymous with that appellation. The estate's history stretches back to the 15th century. Today winemaker François Millet crafts the most elegant and refined wines in Chambolle-Musigny.
lessons.4.slides.2.title: 🏰 Vogüé's Core Holdings
lessons.4.slides.2.points.0: Musigny Grand Cru (7.12 ha) — 70% of total Musigny
lessons.4.slides.2.points.1: Musigny Blanc (0.65 ha) — extremely rare white Musigny
lessons.4.slides.2.points.3: Chambolle-Musigny Les Amoureuses (0.56 ha) — finest Premier Cru
lessons.4.slides.3.title: The 1990s Revival
lessons.4.slides.3.content: Quality at Vogüé slipped in the 1970s and 80s. When François Millet took over in 1986, he launched a thorough overhaul: lower yields, new equipment, improved technique. From the 1990 vintage onwards, quality rose sharply, restoring the estate to the top tier. A reminder that even the greatest terroir needs great management.
lessons.4.slides.4.title: 🍇 Vogüé's Quality Revolution
lessons.4.slides.4.points.0: Lower yields: from 40 hl/ha down to 30 hl/ha
lessons.4.slides.4.points.1: Rigorous sorting: double sorting in vineyard and cellar
lessons.4.slides.4.points.2: Temperature control: modern temperature-control fermentation introduced
lessons.4.slides.4.points.4: Extended ageing: barrel maturation lengthened to 18 months
lessons.4.slides.4.points.5: Later bottling: bottled 6 months later than before
lessons.4.slides.5.title: Musigny vs. Bonnes-Mares
lessons.4.slides.6.title: The Rarity of Musigny Blanc
lessons.4.slides.6.content: Musigny Blanc covers just 0.65 ha and yields roughly 3,000 bottles per year — one of Burgundy's rarest whites. Vogüé holds almost all of it. The wine expresses Chardonnay's ultimate elegance on limestone, and prices rival Le Montrachet. In pursuit of even higher quality, the estate suspended production of Musigny Blanc from 2015 to 2020.
lessons.4.slides.7.title: Vogüé's Quality Revolution Timeline
lessons.4.slides.8.title: Vogüé Before and After the Quality Revolution
lessons.4.slides.9.title: 🧠 Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé Quiz
lessons.5.title: Rising Names: Dujac, Méo-Camuzet
lessons.5.slides.0.title: The Rise of the New Generation
lessons.5.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 6 - 15 minutes
lessons.5.slides.0.description: Discover top estates that rose to prominence in the late 20th century
lessons.5.slides.1.title: Domaine Dujac: Pioneer of Whole-Bunch Fermentation
lessons.5.slides.1.content: Domaine Dujac was founded by Jacques Seysses in 1968, epitomising Burgundy's 'new generation' of estates. Seysses came from outside the wine world, but his passionate pursuit of quality and his innovative spirit made Dujac a top domaine. He is an unwavering advocate of 100% whole-bunch fermentation, believing it adds superior complexity.
lessons.5.slides.2.title: 🌟 Dujac's Core Grand Crus
lessons.5.slides.2.points.0: Clos de la Roche (1.95 ha) — the estate's flagship wine
lessons.5.slides.2.points.1: Clos Saint-Denis (1.46 ha) — elegant and refined
lessons.5.slides.2.points.4: Échézeaux (0.69 ha) — from the Vosne-Romanée side
lessons.5.slides.3.title: Domaine Méo-Camuzet: A Model of Sharecropping Transformation
lessons.5.slides.3.content: Méo-Camuzet has a unique history: for many years its vineyards were run under the métayage (sharecropping) system. In 1988 Jean-Nicolas Méo took direct control and invited legendary winemaker Henri Jayer to mentor him. Jayer's philosophy shaped the domaine's style, and the results are today regarded as some of Burgundy's finest.
lessons.5.slides.4.title: 🍷 Méo-Camuzet's Grand Crus
lessons.5.slides.4.points.1: Clos de Vougeot (3.0 ha) — large holding
lessons.5.slides.4.points.4: Vosne-Romanée Cros Parantoux (0.29 ha) — Premier Cru; Henri Jayer's masterwork
lessons.5.slides.5.title: Dujac vs. Méo-Camuzet
lessons.5.slides.6.title: Henri Jayer's Legacy
lessons.5.slides.6.content: Henri Jayer (1922–2006) is revered as the greatest Burgundy winemaker of the 20th century. His philosophy transformed the entire region: vineyard primacy, low yields, zero destemming, high new oak. Méo-Camuzet, Rouget, and others remain deeply shaped by his thinking. Jayer's Cros Parantoux is one of Burgundy's most legendary Premier Crus.
lessons.5.slides.7.title: Henri Jayer's Influence over Time
lessons.5.slides.8.title: 🎓 Core Tenets of Henri Jayer's Winemaking Philosophy
lessons.5.slides.8.points.0: Vineyard first: 95% of quality comes from the grapes; winemaking contributes just 5%
lessons.5.slides.8.points.1: Ultra-low yields: 25–30 hl/ha, far below legal limits
lessons.5.slides.8.points.2: 100% destemming: he believed whole-bunch fermentation added green notes
lessons.5.slides.8.points.3: Cold maceration: 5–7 days of pre-fermentation cold soaking to extract aromatics
lessons.5.slides.8.points.4: High new oak: 100% new barrels from a specific cooperage
lessons.5.slides.8.points.5: No filtration: preserves every terroir signal and layer of complexity
lessons.5.slides.9.title: Evolution of the Métayage System
lessons.5.slides.10.title: 🧠 Dujac / Méo-Camuzet Quiz
lessons.6.title: Comparative Winemaking Philosophies and Blind Recognition
lessons.6.slides.0.title: Comparing Great Producer Styles
lessons.6.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 7 - 12 minutes
lessons.6.slides.0.description: Learn to recognise the stylistic fingerprints of each estate
lessons.6.slides.1.title: The Winemaking Philosophy Spectrum
lessons.6.slides.1.content: Top Burgundy estates sit across a wide spectrum — from the ultra-traditional (Rousseau) to the innovative modern (Méo-Camuzet), from minimum intervention (Leroy) to precise technical control (DRC). Understanding these differences enables us to identify producer styles in blind tasting.
lessons.6.slides.2.title: 🔬 Key Winemaking Parameter Comparison
lessons.6.slides.2.points.0: Whole-bunch: DRC 100% | Dujac 100% | Rousseau 50–70% | Méo 0–50% | Jayer 0%
lessons.6.slides.2.points.1: New oak: DRC 100% | Méo 80–100% | Dujac 50–60% | Rousseau 30–50% | Coche 20–30%
lessons.6.slides.2.points.2: Yields: Leroy 15 hl/ha | DRC 20–25 | Jayer 25–30 | Rousseau 28–32
lessons.6.slides.2.points.3: Biodynamic: Leroy and DRC fully certified; others partial or not
lessons.6.slides.2.points.4: Filtration: DRC, Leroy, Jayer — none; others — case by case
lessons.6.slides.2.points.5: Barrel ageing: DRC 18 months | Coche 18 months | typical estate 12–16 months
lessons.6.slides.3.title: Blind Recognition: Whole-Bunch vs. Destemmed
lessons.6.slides.4.title: 👁️ Advanced Blind Tasting Recognition Keys
lessons.6.slides.4.points.0: DRC: ethereal elegance, multi-layered, whole-bunch spice + perfect balance + extremely long finish
lessons.6.slides.4.points.1: Leroy: extreme concentration, deep, firm young tannins + super density + needs 20 years
lessons.6.slides.4.points.2: Rousseau: power and elegance balanced, pure fruit, moderate whole-bunch, perfect extraction
lessons.6.slides.4.points.3: Coche-Dury (white): profound complexity, mineral + creamy texture + nuts and honey
lessons.6.slides.4.points.4: Vogüé: silken texture, extreme elegance, floral-dominant (Musigny hallmark)
lessons.6.slides.4.points.5: Dujac: aroma-driven, prominent florals, 100% whole-bunch, carnation and rose
lessons.6.slides.4.points.6: Méo-Camuzet: rich fruit, silky tannins, high oak, generous but not heavy
lessons.6.slides.4.points.7: Recognition order: first assess whole-bunch % → then evaluate new oak → lastly check concentration
lessons.6.slides.5.title: Traditional vs. Modern
lessons.6.slides.6.title: There Is No Absolute 'Best'
lessons.6.slides.6.content: Every top producer has a distinct philosophy and style — there is no absolute 'best'. DRC pursues terroir purity; Leroy pursues extreme concentration; Rousseau pursues the balance of power and elegance; Coche-Dury pursues depth in white wine. Understanding and appreciating these differences is what it means to be a true Burgundy lover.
lessons.6.slides.7.title: 💡 Learning Recommendations
lessons.6.slides.7.points.0: Taste side-by-side wines from different producers in the same village whenever possible
lessons.6.slides.7.points.1: Notice the effect of whole-bunch fermentation: spice, florals, tannin texture
lessons.6.slides.7.points.2: Pay attention to new-oak levels: vanilla, toasted bread, smoke
lessons.6.slides.7.points.3: Compare different vintages to see how each estate responds to climate variation
lessons.6.slides.7.points.4: Read producer interviews to understand the thinking behind their winemaking philosophy
lessons.6.slides.8.title: 🧠 Winemaking Philosophy Comparison and Blind Recognition Quiz
